item.title: New Study Shows How Young People Feel About AI Companions
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from 404 Media: A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion. Gallup's study is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children's Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries. A lot of the topline results won't surprise anyone living in today's constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling. Young people in the United States, Canada, and UK reported the least interest in AI overall, with only 20% saying they used it once a day or more. Almost 40 percent of young people in Brazil use it daily. Japan and Italy both come in around 35%. "Nearly half of young people in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada have used AI no more than a few times in the past month, including those who have not used it at all," the researchers wrote. Most of the respondents (82%) said they'd used AI to look up information, 68% asked it for advice, and 33% used it as a companion. Young people with online-only friends were more likely to use AI for companionship, "although these patterns do not establish whether AI companionship supplements or substitutes for human relationships," they wrote. The researchers discovered that people in different countries felt wildly different about their AI buddies. Almost half of Australians with AI friends rated the relationship as "high quality" and only 12% of young people in Poland did. Mostly, though, people thought of their AI friends as mid: "In most countries [...] young people are more likely to give their AI companionship a medium rating than either a high or low rating." People who used AI as a friend also reported higher levels of loneliness, the study found. "However, the findings cannot determine whether young people turn to AI because they feel lonely, whether AI companionship influences their social experiences or whether other circumstances help explain these relationships," the researchers wrote. [...] The study's authors warned about reading too much into these results. "These assessments should be compared cautiously with those for human friendships examined in this report, as young people may have different expectations of what makes an AI companion or human friendship meaningful or supportive," the researchers wrote. "The broader message is not that one form of connection is inherently better or worse, but that the quality of young people's relationships and the wider social context in which they exist matter greatly," the study concluded.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

item.title: Ancient minerals reveal a missing chapter in Türkiye's mountain-building history
item.description: A mountain range can bear the marks of events from tens of millions of years ago. The challenge lies in determining when each mark was created. In southern Türkiye's Central Taurides, scientists have developed a method to date some of these ancient movements by examining tiny calcite deposits that formed as faults shifted. This new timeline alters the region's geological history. Researchers discovered a previously unrecognized period during which parts of the crust slid laterally, between the Early Eocene and Early Miocene. They also found that the region's later extension began around 25 million years ago, earlier than previously believed.

item.title: New mixing benchmark could help industry reduce energy use in stirred tanks

Floating particles often pose a challenge in mixing because they are lighter than the liquid and tend to float at its surface. While impeller agitation does draw them into the liquid, the minimum mixing intensity needed for effective drawdown has been difficult to define.

item.title: Atoms in sync: Superradiance offers a new kind of frequency comb
item.description: When scientists shine a laser beam into a crystal, they typically expect a steady glow as the crystal's atoms are energized and begin to emit light. But in early 2024, while searching for something else entirely, researchers in the lab of Caltech's Andrei Faraon saw a crystal flash in a regular rhythm, like a metronome keeping a beat. The flashes came from billions of atoms embedded in the crystal. Coupled to a tiny superconducting circuit, the atoms had become synchronized and started emitting light together through a special quantum phenomenon known as superradiance.

The retailer currently offers a limited selection of 15 Blu-ray listings, including new releases like The Odyssey and Project Hail Mary and older titles like It's a Wonderful Life (1943), Saving Private Ryan (1998), and The Godfather (1972). Ars Technica reports: Overall, the sales of Blu-rays and DVDs in the US have been steadily declining, and annual consumer spending dropped 9.3 percent from 2024 to 2025, according to the Digital Entertainment Group (DEG). During this same time, however, consumer spending on 4K Blu-ray discs specifically increased 12 percent year over year, per DEG. "We're seeing a lot of evidence, including at the Criterion Mobile Closet, that more young people are thinking about physical media in a different way," Peter Becker, president of Criterion, which sells Blu-rays and DVDs online, told the Los Angeles Times in February. item.title: Bank CEOs, NSA Tell Congress That AI-Driven Patches Are Behind Outages
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Washington Sun: Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency have told members of Congress that this week's widespread tech outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities identified by artificial intelligence, according to three sources familiar with the private conversations. [...] "These models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, and that increases the urgency to patch right away," said one congressional official briefed on the matter. "They're trying to push through a lot of patches all at once -- more than the system was designed for." On Monday, banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs for the service issues. On Tuesday, the NSA said that "scheduled routine maintenance" was responsible for the "temporary degradation" of some of its networks. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC on Tuesday that "they're pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system. ... We're going to see more of this as new technology rolls out." "There's some sense in which this is reassuring, in that it means there's not an attack. But it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure we rely on is based on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems," said Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at Encode. "Updating those is going to be a rocky process, and as we get more advanced models this won't be a one and done thing -- we'll continue to find more vulnerabilities."

item.title: Build a Personal Brand to Help Employers Find You
item.description:
This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!In one year, the number of developers working for themselves has more than doubled. Stack Overflow’s annual survey of more than 30,000 developers showed that freelancers and sole proprietors went from about four percent of respondents to ten percent.

You can read this as a polite way of saying, “I got laid off and I’m figuring it out.” But I don’t think the number can be ignored.

Whatever the case, it leads to the question I keep hearing from engineers right now: What can I do to stay employable? One tried and true answer is to build a personal brand.

But what does that actually mean?

Over the last six years, I grew my LinkedIn audience to 40,000 followers and YouTube channel to 10,000. I don’t think you should aim to be famous (unless you’re into that sort of thing) but I do think it’s worth exploring how to be discoverable online in 2027 if you want an advantage in the open market.

A personal brand is a discovery mechanism

Strip away the follower counts and the AI-generated thought leadership, and a personal brand comes down to a simple question: Does the internet know who you are? When a hiring manager goes looking for someone who has your skills, do you show up?

You can think of this as search engine optimization for your employability. Recruiters have mostly consolidated around a single platform to find people: LinkedIn.

Those 40,000 followers and millions of impressions came with barely a viral post to my name. Nobody is begging me to do sponsorships. But I rarely have trouble finding work, and far more opportunities come to me than I go looking for. That has much less to do with fame than with being easy to find.

You don’t need 10,000 followers. You need a trail of breadcrumbs.

Don’t write AI slop

LinkedIn is notorious for being overrun with AI-generated posts. It’s become a running joke. That’s good news for you, because the bar to stand out is “sound like a human being.”

Write about what you actually achieved: a hairy bug you squashed, how your team handles deployments, why you picked some obscure library, the migration that went sideways at 2 a.m. Specifics are hard to fake and easy to trust. (But be careful not to post sensitive information.)

And post a picture of yourself once in a while. People connect with faces a lot faster than with walls of text.

Hot takes, with caution

Posts with an opinion tend to outperform tutorials, but you don’t have to dunk on anyone to have one. For instance, if you work on a tech stack people love to mock (VB, .NET, some ancient Java monolith held together with prayer), try something like “What people get wrong about .NET.”

You’ll attract a few trolls in the comments—free engagement, honestly—plus people who want an actual conversation. These comments can turn into actual connections and even… friends.

A routine you can follow

Posting twice a week is not a big ask. Pick a simple, repeatable format so you’re never staring at an empty text box: what you worked on, what broke, and what you learned. Even a post that gets 10 views leaves one more breadcrumb about who you are and what you know.

Over time, the people who comment become your network. And because so few engineers post about their work on LinkedIn, you can become a big fish in a small pond surprisingly fast.

Write for the people a few steps behind you

The best audience is engineers one or two steps behind where you are now. Answer the questions you had a year ago. It helps them, it sharpens your own thinking, and every so often it turns into mentorship in both directions.

It also tells a future employer more about how you think than any résumé bullet ever could.

The engineers who grab the most opportunities are the ones employers can find. You don’t need to become an influencer to be one of them. You just need to leave enough breadcrumbs that the right person can follow them back to you.

—Brian

item.title: Jensen Huang's Fall Hits 'Open' Models In Boost to Anthropic and OpenAI
item.description:
Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia could weaken the open AI model ecosystem he spent years championing, potentially strengthening closed-model developers like OpenAI and Anthropic, according to the Financial Times. From the report: The US chip giant's former chief threw Nvidia's balance sheet into creating a broad AI ecosystem, including by seeding and acquiring start-ups involved in the development of open-source and open-weight models, which users can customize and run on their own hardware. Huang was a forceful advocate for their spread, lobbying against Washington's moves to restrict the use of Chinese-made open models while seeking the development of US alternatives. "Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector," he wrote this summer in his first-ever message on X. His ignominious exit from Nvidia deprives the open model sector of its most vocal and influential supporter in the US. "I think Jensen stood to gain the most economically and was personally committed to diversity at the model layer," said one venture capitalist who has invested in AI start-ups alongside Nvidia. "Without him and a less generous Nvidia in terms of investment, we may end up in a much more concentrated world of model providers." Whether Nvidia will continue the rapid pace of dealmaking under a new leader is unclear. The company was expected to participate in or lead four start-up deals currently under discussion: investments in Thinking Machines Lab and Groq, a potential partnership with Reflection AI and the $12.9bn acquisition of open model repository Hugging Face. "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," said Elon Musk in a post on X on Saturday. "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost." "In some sense [Huang leaving Nvidia] is bad for the industry, but in some sense Jensen is an enemy of the frontier labs because he wants models to become commoditized so he retains the prime position in the value chain," said one senior figure at a leading Silicon Valley AI company. "I don't think open weight models are going away... but losing Jensen as their greatest financial backer and champion will slow their progress, and I imagine will not hurt Anthropic's IPO," said another industry figure. "It's reasonable to expect the ouster of Jensen will concentrate computing power more in the hands of frontier labs and hyperscalers," added a senior figure at an AI lab. "That's good for the labs."

item.title: Satya Nadella Says He's AGI-Pilled Now
item.description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Verge: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he's AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. "I am AGI-pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy's organization around AGI?" he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco. But Nadella doesn't think frontier models like Claude are conscious. "I don't think so," he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman's view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic's team has "wireheaded" themselves, and that this approach is dangerous. Nadella wasn't quite as firm about it. "It's a good debate," he said. "I'm not sort of dogmatic about it. What I'm saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?" I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter's questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status. "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us." "Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be," he said. "But remember, the model has no limits. It'll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it." Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. "If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?" he asked. "If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That's the debate." "I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one -- at least in a democracy -- can even win an election if this just goes that way, if there's only capital and there's no labor. I mean, I don't know, that's not an economy." "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us. Not just for me. You are also going to somehow be some affiliate of Anthropic."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

item.title: Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day From Earth
item.description:
NASA's Voyager 1 has become the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth, or 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). This means radio signals will take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft, now nearly 50 years into its mission. "Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal -- so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky," reports Space.com. From the report: But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA. [...] At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Big Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Hill: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.'s measles elimination status, ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in modern history. The U.S. met with PAHO's Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission for a three-day, closed-door meeting last week. "The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted," Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO's director, said during the briefing Tuesday. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000 and has held onto that for more than 25 years. But the past two years have seen close to 8,000 measles infections and roughly a dozen related deaths. This year has been the worst in terms of transmission in more than 30 years. Erica Schwartz, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has previously said losing elimination status won't lead to changes in the federal response. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities," Schwartz said on Tuesday. "Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks."

item.title: New model reveals how water moves through tile-drained farm fields
item.description: Tile drainage fundamentally alters how water moves through agricultural fields, affecting surface ponding, water-table dynamics, crop growth, nutrient transport and water quality. Yet fields with similar drainage systems can respond differently depending on soil, topography and tile design—differences that most models struggle to resolve at the field scale.

item.title: NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound
item.description: NASA has successfully tested Mars helicopter rotor blades at supersonic speeds, boosting potential lift by 30% and overcoming a major obstacle to more powerful aircraft on the Red Planet. The breakthrough could enable next-generation helicopters to carry heavier scientific equipment, fly farther, and explore places beyond the reach of traditional rovers.

item.title: An atlas of vanished places: How climate change is rewriting the books on our shelves
item.description: On Aug. 26, 2026, a huge mass of rock and ice broke away at an altitude of around 5,200 meters (17,100 feet) in the Himalayas. Within minutes, it became an avalanche of debris and water that hurtled down toward the Nepal-Tibet border, with such force that the seismic signals were initially mistaken for an earthquake.

item.title: New research finds AI adoption is associated with more managers—and different managerial skills
item.description: A Strategic Management Journal study challenges the assumption that AI adoption automatically reduces demand for managers. Liudmila Alekseeva, José Azar, Mireia Giné and Sampsa Samila analyze U.S. job postings from 2010 to 2022, linking firm-level AI adoption with managerial vacancies and skill requirements.

item.title: Invasive plants show limited spread in Andalusia's mountains
item.description: A study by the University of Córdoba (UCO) departments of Forest Engineering and of Botany, Ecology and Plant Physiology reveals that the presence of invasive plants in Sierra Nevada and the Sierra de los Filabres—two mountain ecosystems in Andalusia that are especially vulnerable to climate change and home to unique plant species—is currently low. Specifically, invasive plants are most common in the areas closest to the edges of roads, and their presence declines at the highest points of the mountains.

item.title: COP31: How to make carbon markets more effective
item.description: At the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, a key question for negotiators is how to get more money to developing countries so they can adapt to a warming world. For the past 30 years, climate talks focused on cutting greenhouse gas emissions and preventing future global warming.

item.title: 125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert
item.description: A remarkable 125,000-year-old discovery in Saudi Arabia reveals that early humans once thrived beside enormous lakes filled with wildlife in what is now a vast desert. Thousands of stone tools and ancient plant remains suggest these prehistoric people used sophisticated hunting techniques, potentially including weapons enhanced with poisonous plant compounds.

item.title: Gender differences in values are not widening in Europe after all
item.description: In recent years, public discussion has focused on the increasingly conservative values of young men. A recently published study indicates that this is primarily a phenomenon prominent in social and conventional media, not an overall trend.

item.title: Nvidia Rejects Jensen Huang's Offer to Return as CEO
item.description:
Nvidia's board has unanimously rejected former CEO Jensen Huang's offer to return, despite public support from President Trump and prominent Silicon Valley figures. The decision came as Nvidia reported blockbuster third-quarter revenue of $116 billion, double the year-earlier figure. The Associated Press reports: The embattled company's board of directors "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of Nvidia's quarterly earnings call before yielding to Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who is running the company as a permanent replacement is sought. [...] Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said in a social media post that if the board decided that his return was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and the country, he would be "honored to answer these calls." He acknowledged making "serious mistakes" in his personal life. The turmoil notwithstanding, Nvidia blew past Wall Street expectations for the third quarter, pulling in $116 billion in revenue, double the level from a year ago. The company also posted net income of $2.70 per share, beating estimates of $2.48 per share. Nvidia stock shot up 5.2% in after-hours trading. Referring to Huang's replacement, Jones said, "We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person." Nvidia also announced a new board committee overseeing national security and trade compliance amid investigations into alleged AI chip smuggling to China. item.title: How restaurants can make sustainable dining choices easier while still making a profit
item.description: Canadians are eating out less. A 2025 survey found 57% of them are cooking at home more often to save money, while 69% of restaurant operators say customers are dining out less because of affordability. According to Restaurants Canada, 41% of operators are either losing money or breaking even.

item.title: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
item.description: Scientists discovered that although people with and without autism show surprisingly similar average brain activity, individuals with autism exhibit much greater differences from one another, especially in regions involved in social understanding. The findings suggest that traditional research methods may be overlooking crucial differences that could help unlock more personalized autism support.
